title: What is eBPF-based observability and when do you reach for it beyond APM — APM/metrics/traces see the application and JVM, but eBPF runs sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel to see what's below it (syscalls, TCP retransmits / packet drops, run-queue / scheduler latency, disk I/O waits, page faults) with no code changes or agents (tools like bpftrace/bcc, Pixie, Cilium) — useful when latency spikes or pod restarts have no application-level cause?
shortTitle: eBPF-based observability and when to reach for it beyond APM

s1_definition.profdef: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a Linux kernel technology that lets you attach small, sandboxed, verified programs to kernel hooks — system calls, network events, scheduler events, disk I/O — so you can observe and measure what the operating system is doing with no changes to application code and no instrumentation agent inside the app. eBPF-based observability uses this to surface kernel-level signals like TCP retransmits and packet drops, run-queue and scheduler latency, disk I/O wait, and page faults. You reach for it beyond APM when a latency spike or a pod restart has no visible cause at the application or JVM level, because the real cause lives below the application in the kernel, the network, or the host.
s1_definition.analogy: Normal application monitoring, called APM, is like watching the clerks at the National Bank of India — you see how fast each clerk serves Rajesh and Priya and whether they make mistakes. But sometimes the clerk is fast and correct, yet customers still wait, because the problem is beneath the clerk: the building's elevators are slow, the phone lines keep dropping, or the back-office mail room is jammed. APM cannot see any of that. eBPF is like installing silent sensors in the building's infrastructure itself — the elevators, the phone exchange, the mail room — without disturbing a single clerk. When customers are mysteriously slow and every clerk looks fine, those infrastructure sensors reveal that the phone lines are dropping and being redialed, which was invisible from the clerk's desk.
s1_definition.oneliner: eBPF runs safe sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel to reveal syscalls, network drops, scheduler and disk waits with zero app changes — reach for it when a latency spike or restart has no application-level explanation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a Linux kernel technology that lets you attach small, sandboxed, verified programs to kernel hooks — system calls, network events, scheduler events, disk I/O — so you can observe and measure what the operating system is doing with no changes to application code and no instrumentation agent inside the app. eBPF-based observability uses this to surface kernel-level signals like TCP retransmits and packet drops, run-queue and scheduler latency, disk I/O wait, and page faults. You reach for it beyond APM when a latency spike or a pod restart has no visible cause at the application or JVM level, because the real cause lives below the application in the kernel, the network, or the host.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Normal application monitoring, called APM, is like watching the clerks at the National Bank of India — you see how fast each clerk serves Rajesh and Priya and whether they make mistakes. But sometimes the clerk is fast and correct, yet customers still wait, because the problem is beneath the clerk: the building's elevators are slow, the phone lines keep dropping, or the back-office mail room is jammed. APM cannot see any of that. eBPF is like installing silent sensors in the building's infrastructure itself — the elevators, the phone exchange, the mail room — without disturbing a single clerk. When customers are mysteriously slow and every clerk looks fine, those infrastructure sensors reveal that the phone lines are dropping and being redialed, which was invisible from the clerk's desk.

**One line to remember:** eBPF runs safe sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel to reveal syscalls, network drops, scheduler and disk waits with zero app changes — reach for it when a latency spike or restart has no application-level explanation.

sections.s2_technical:
APM, metrics, and traces instrument the application. They see request rates, error rates, latency, database calls, and JVM internals like heap and garbage collection. This covers most problems, but it has a blind spot: everything below the application. When your code is fast, your JVM is healthy, and your traces show the time is spent "somewhere" that no span captures, the cause is in the layer APM cannot reach — the kernel, the network stack, the scheduler, or the disk.

eBPF fills that gap. The Linux kernel exposes hook points, and eBPF lets you attach a tiny program to a hook such as a system call entry or exit, a network packet event, a scheduler context switch, or a block-device I/O completion. The program runs in kernel space but is first checked by the eBPF verifier, which guarantees it cannot crash the kernel, cannot loop forever, and cannot access memory it should not — this safety is what makes running code in the kernel acceptable in production. The program gathers data into efficient kernel maps that user-space tools read. Crucially, this requires no change to your application and no agent library linked into your process; you load the eBPF program on the host and it observes everything.

The signals eBPF exposes are exactly the ones APM misses. TCP retransmits and packet drops reveal a flaky network or an overloaded peer that makes requests silently slow because packets are being re-sent. Run-queue latency — the scheduler delay — reveals that your process was ready to run but the CPU was busy with something else, so your "slow" request was actually waiting for CPU time, not doing work. Disk I/O wait reveals that a read or write blocked on slow storage. Page faults reveal memory pressure causing the kernel to fetch pages. Syscall latency reveals time spent in kernel operations like file or socket calls. None of these show up as an application span, yet any of them can be the true cause of a latency spike.

The tooling has matured. bpftrace and BCC are the low-level, ad-hoc tools — you write a short script to trace, say, every TCP retransmit or the distribution of run-queue latency, and get answers in minutes. Pixie gives Kubernetes a no-instrumentation observability layer built on eBPF, automatically capturing service-to-service traffic, latency, and resource usage without touching the apps. Cilium uses eBPF for networking, security, and network observability in Kubernetes, giving you a map of actual pod-to-pod traffic and drops. These tools let you answer kernel-level questions in production without redeploying anything.

When do you reach for it beyond APM? The trigger is a symptom with no application-level cause. Latency spikes while the application and JVM look perfectly healthy, pods restarting without any application error, intermittent slowness that correlates with no code path, or network weirdness between services that traces cannot explain. In those cases you use eBPF to look below the application — check for TCP retransmits between the pods, measure scheduler latency to see if the node is CPU-starved, check disk I/O wait, and inspect page-fault rates. A senior nuance: eBPF is powerful but it is a specialist tool, not a replacement for metrics, logs, and traces — you still start with the three pillars, and you drop down to eBPF only when those pillars point "below the application" without pinpointing the cause. It is also kernel-version and privilege sensitive, so you use managed tools like Pixie or Cilium in production rather than hand-loading raw programs everywhere.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service shows intermittent latency spikes. The APM dashboard is maddening: request rate normal, error rate zero, JVM heap healthy, garbage collection quiet, and the traces show the time is spent inside a call to the account service but no span explains why. The on-call engineer needs to look below the application.

Problem 1 — The engineer first confirms the application layer is clean: the trace shows the account-service call took 800 milliseconds, but the account service's own trace says it processed in 20 milliseconds. The missing 780 milliseconds vanished between the two services — a network-level problem APM cannot see.

Problem 2 — Using eBPF, the engineer traces TCP retransmits between the transfer pod and the account pod and finds a storm of retransmits, meaning packets are being dropped and re-sent, which silently inflates latency.

Problem 3 — The engineer also checks run-queue latency and finds the node is CPU-saturated by a noisy neighbour pod, adding scheduler delay. Both causes are below the application.

Our runnable Java simulation models an eBPF-style probe layer: `AppLayerView` (what APM sees), and `KernelLayerProbe` (what eBPF sees — TCP retransmits, run-queue latency, disk I/O wait, page faults). A `RootCauseAnalyzer` compares them: when the app layer is clean but latency is high, it drops to the kernel probe to find the cause. Classes: `AppLayerView`, `KernelLayerProbe`, `RootCauseAnalyzer`, and an `EbpfDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — a real bpftrace one-liner script

```bash
# bpf/tcp_retransmit.bt — eBPF program: count TCP retransmits by destination.
# No app changes, no agent in the JVM — this runs in the kernel.
#!/usr/bin/env bpftrace
kprobe:tcp_retransmit_skb
{
    @retransmits[comm, ntop(((struct sock *)arg0)->__sk_common.skc_daddr)] = count();
}
interval:s:5
{
    time("%H:%M:%S TCP retransmits (process, dest) in last 5s:\n");
    print(@retransmits);
    clear(@retransmits);
}
# Run:  sudo bpftrace bpf/tcp_retransmit.bt
# Other useful eBPF probes:
#   runqlat   -> run-queue (scheduler) latency histogram
#   biolatency-> block I/O (disk) latency histogram
#   execsnoop -> every process exec (debug mysterious restarts)
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer latency spike where the caller's trace measured 800 milliseconds for the account-service call, but the account service self-reported only 20 milliseconds, leaving a 780-millisecond gap, while heap, GC, and error rate all look healthy.

Step 1: The analyzer reads the application-layer view. It computes the unexplained gap of 780 milliseconds and confirms the application layer looks clean — zero errors, healthy heap, quiet garbage collection. APM alone is a dead end here.

Step 2: Because the app is clean yet latency is high, the analyzer drops to the eBPF kernel probes. This is the key decision: the cause must be below the application, so it looks at kernel-level signals that APM cannot see.

Step 3: The kernel probe reports 180 TCP retransmits in five seconds between the transfer pod and the account pod. This is flagged severe — packets are being dropped and re-sent, which silently inflates latency without any application error. This explains a large part of the missing 780 milliseconds.

Step 4: The kernel probe also reports run-queue latency of 35 milliseconds, flagged severe as CPU starvation — the process was ready to run but waited for the CPU because a noisy neighbour pod was consuming it. Disk I/O wait and page faults are within normal range, so they are not the cause.

Step 5: The analyzer concludes the root cause lives below the application, invisible to APM alone. The fix is to move the noisy-neighbour pod off the node and investigate the flaky network path, after which the transfer latency returns to normal.

```
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — transfer latency spike with clean APM
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [INFO   ] APM view: observed latency 800ms, unexplained gap 780ms
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [WARNING] APM shows NO application-level cause but latency is high -> dropping to eBPF kernel probes (below the app)
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [SEVERE ] eBPF: 180 TCP retransmits/5s — packet drops re-sending, silent latency
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [SEVERE ] eBPF: run-queue latency 35ms — CPU-starved by a noisy neighbour, request waited for CPU
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [INFO   ] Root cause found BELOW the application — invisible to APM alone.
2026-10-30 02:18:55 [INFO   ] Fix: move noisy-neighbour pod off this node, investigate flaky NIC/overlay; transfer SAV2001->CUR3001 latency returns to normal.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
eBPF is a Linux kernel technology that lets you attach small, sandboxed, verified programs to kernel hook points such as system calls, network events, scheduler context switches, and disk I/O, so you can observe what the operating system is doing with no changes to application code and no agent inside the process. The programs are checked by the eBPF verifier before they run, which guarantees they cannot crash the kernel or loop forever, and that safety is what makes running code in the kernel acceptable in production. eBPF-based observability uses this to surface signals like TCP retransmits and packet drops, run-queue or scheduler latency, disk I/O wait, and page faults.

The reason it matters is that normal APM, metrics, and traces only see the application and the JVM. They tell you request rates, error rates, latency, database calls, heap, and garbage collection, which covers most problems, but they have a blind spot for everything below the application. When your code is fast, your JVM is healthy, and the trace shows the time is spent somewhere that no span captures, the cause is in the kernel, the network stack, the scheduler, or the disk — and APM simply cannot see it. That is exactly when I reach for eBPF.

In my project at the National Bank of India, the transfer service had intermittent latency spikes that were maddening because APM was spotless: zero errors, healthy heap, quiet garbage collection. But a trace showed the account-service call took 800 milliseconds while the account service itself reported only 20 milliseconds, so 780 milliseconds vanished between the two services. Dropping to eBPF, I traced TCP retransmits between the transfer pod and the account pod and found a storm of retransmits — packets were being dropped and re-sent, silently inflating latency — and I measured run-queue latency and found the node was CPU-starved by a noisy neighbour pod, so requests were waiting for CPU rather than doing work. Both causes were below the application and invisible to APM. I used bpftrace and BCC tools for the ad-hoc investigation, and in Kubernetes I rely on Pixie and Cilium with Hubble for no-instrumentation kernel and network observability. The principle I always state is that eBPF is an escalation, not a replacement — I start with the three pillars, and when they point below the application without pinpointing the cause, eBPF lets me see into the kernel with zero code changes.
